corrected_content.problem:
![](images/df/df940d9ea08ed1b326d4904933bd41c318112836d2d657abcb3c158aabbe7bb4.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $\mathbf{r}(t)=3\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{i}+2\operatorname{sin}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{j}$ 
for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
corrected_content.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}2t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}2t\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-12{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =12{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =4{{u}^{3}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$
